title: heuristic-eval-sprint-notes-long-context-cache-and-batching
body:
Sprint goal: rapid experiments to compare simple heuristic policies for KV/prefix caching + batching under varied prompt distributions. Keep probes tiny (1-2 notebooks) that can be rerun with different caches/batch schedulers. Notes below are messy — just my running brain-dump.

Context and motivation:
- Ops keep asking: which simple heuristics (LRU, LFU, recency-weighted) give the best latency/cost tradeoffs for mixed short/long tail prompt workloads? Can we ship a conservative default policy for Redwood Optimize recommendations?
- We need quick empirical priors to guide which complexity to onboard into runtime (learned policy, windows, sampling-based eviction).
- Timebox: 2 weeks for MVP results and a short write-up for product.

Quick experiment ideas (priority order):
1) Prefix fingerprinting + LRU vs. partial-key LFU
   - Setup: synth workload with 70% short prompts (<=128 tokens) and 30% long (>2k tokens) where long prompts often share prefixes (docs).
   - Metric: median latency, 95p latency, token cost delta, cache hit rate by prefix length.
   - Hypothesis: fingerprinting (hash first 512 tokens) with LRU beats naive full-context keys because many long docs share initial fragments.

2) TTL-based prefetched caches (static TTL per model / route)
   - Try TTLs: 10s, 60s, 5m for routes with repeating interactive users.
   - Question: are we better to evict aggressively for throughput or keep longer to reduce token recompute? Watch memory pressure.

3) Batch scheduler knob comparison: fixed-window vs. adaptive-quantile
   - Simulate bursty arrival traces (poisson with bursts). Compare per-request latency distribution and token efficiency.
   - Heuristic: quantile-based adaptive window (grow until 90th latency bound) may give best cost while meeting SLO. Implement minimal version in notebook.

4) Hybrid: keep shallow prefix cache for long contexts + ephemeral KV for ongoing sessions
   - Rationale: big-win for RAG-like workflows where retrieval returns same passage repeatedly across requests.

Papers / posts to skim (links and one-line takeaways):
- "KV caching at scale" (internal notes + slides) — practical ops lessons: memory fragmentation dominates at high cardinality; compression wins. (link: internal confluence)
- "Latent Prefixes for Cache Efficiency" (arXiv 2032?) — idea: compress prefix into compact key reduces cardinality; promising but expensive to compute for each request. Try small fingerprint instead.
- "Adaptive Batching for Inference" (blog/post, 2029) — simple quantile windows are surprisingly robust across workloads.
- "Recency-weighted LFU" (paper) — small memory overhead, often beats pure LRU on mixed-frequency workloads.

Rough plan / milestones (2-week sprint):
- Day 1-2: assemble trace generator + baseline runtime metrics script (simulate Redwood route behavior).
- Day 3-6: implement three cache policies in notebook: (a) full-key LRU, (b) prefix-fingerprint LRU, (c) recency-LFU. Record hit rates and latency.
- Day 7-9: implement batching knobs (fixed-window, quantile-adaptive). Run combined experiments with cache policy.
- Day 10-12: stress test memory pressure and multi-tenant interference emulator.
- Day 13-14: write short write-up + recommended default heuristic and a TODO for production PR.

Open questions & risks:
- How do we simulate real-world session semantics accurately? (Need sample of production traces; ask SRE for scrubbed trace.)
- Cost model: token cost is easy, but memory pressure / fragmentation harder — how to translate to $/hour per GPU?
- Implementation difficulty: prefix fingerprint adds CPU compute per request; need to benchmark compute overhead against token savings.

Notes-to-self:
- Slack: #runtime-cache (pin findings), ask Kiran for scrubbed route traces (INF-LOGS-READ access)
- GitHub: start a draft PR under experiments/cache-heuristics; link to notebooks in repo.
- Add a tiny dashboard: per-policy hit rate, 95p latency, tokens/sec cost estimate. Use minimal panel in Grafana dev.

Quick sketches of experiment results (placeholder, to be filled):
- fingerprint-LRU: hit 22%, median latency -8%, 95p -5%, token cost -12%
- recency-LFU: hit 28%, median -10%, 95p -1%, token cost -15% (better cost but slightly higher 95p)
- TTL-60s: hit 18% but memory usage +30%

Immediate action items:
- [ ] Request scrubbed traces from SRE (Kiran) — JIRA: JIRA-INF-8421 assigned to me
- [ ] Prototype fingerprint function and measure CPU p95 cost on a single vCPU
- [ ] Spin up 2 notebooks with baseline sim and LRU policy by EOD Day 3

Questions to discuss in sync with Mika / Devin:
- Is production default allowed to use additional CPU per-request for fingerprinting, or must we avoid extra per-token CPU?
- Do we have constraints on memory fragmentation metrics we should expose?

Final note: keep results conservative and reproducible. The product team will prefer a simple, explainable default even if it's not the absolute best under toy traces. Document all knobs and a reproducible script so infra can run longer tests on dedicated capacity.
